prompt:
Extract every policy commitment stated in the text below.

Rules:
- One commitment per line.
- Write each as a verb phrase: an action followed by its object. For example: "raise the income tax threshold" or "build 300000 new homes".
- State each commitment at the level of a distinct policy action, not its implementation details. Do not subdivide a single commitment into steps.
- Include every commitment. Do not select, rank, prioritise, or judge importance.
- Use the text's own terms for policy objects. Do not substitute synonyms.
- Do not number the lines. No bullets, headings, preamble, or commentary.
- If the text states no policy commitments, output the single word NONE.

<text>
Summary (≤500 words)

The manifesto proposes a jobs‑focused economic upgrade funded by a National Transformation Fund (£250bn over 10 years) and a National Investment Bank with regional banks to expand patient lending, especially to SMEs and R&D. Fiscal plans include eliminating the day‑to‑day deficit within five years, lowering debt by the end of the Parliament, and strengthening the budget watchdog. Tax changes: no rises in income tax below £80k, nor in personal NICs or VAT; higher rates for top earners; a higher corporation tax for large firms while restoring a lower small‑profits rate; stronger anti‑avoidance enforcement.

Industrial measures set missions for 60% zero‑carbon/renewable energy by 2030 and R&D at 3% of GDP by 2030. Major infrastructure: HS2 to Scotland, “Crossrail of the North,” Crossrail 2, a new Brighton Main Line, an Oxford–Cambridge arc, nationwide rail electrification; universal superfast broadband by 2022, wider 4G and uninterrupted 5G on key corridors. Public procurement would require fair tax, prompt payment, workforce, and environmental standards. Utilities to be returned to public ownership over time (rail as franchises expire; energy networks; water; postal service). Business reforms include stakeholder duties for directors, takeover safeguards, curbs on excessive pay, business rates reform, and strict action on late payments.

Energy policy: an immediate price cap while moving to a publicly owned, decentralised, low‑carbon system; insulation for 4m homes; interest‑free loans for homeowners; higher standards for rented homes; ban on fracking; support for CCS, renewables (including tidal) and nuclear. Seek continued access to the Internal Energy Market and Euratom.

Brexit stance: accept the result; prioritise jobs and living standards; seek the benefits of the Single Market and Customs Union; guarantee rights for EU and UK nationals; reject “no deal”; avoid a hard Irish border; ensure a meaningful parliamentary vote; retain cooperation with EU agencies and programmes.

Work and welfare: a 20‑point plan including day‑one rights, a ban on zero‑hours contracts, a real Living Wage (target £10 by 2020), removal of employment tribunal fees, extended paternity leave, fair pay ratios in the public sector and for public contractors, and sectoral collective bargaining. Clampdown on bogus self‑employment and reform of employment status law. Pensions protected by the triple lock; review of pension age based on work conditions and life expectancy. Social security changes include scrapping sanctions and the bedroom tax, redesigning Universal Credit (ending six‑week waits and the two‑child limit), and overhauling disability assessments while incorporating the UN disability convention into law.

Housing: over 1m new homes, including at least 100k social homes per year by the end of the Parliament; new towns; brownfield priority; strengthened standards; leasehold reforms; three‑year private tenancies with inflation‑capped rent rises; ban on letting fees; tougher landlord standards; expanded action on homelessness.

Public services: NHS funding uplift of over £30bn over the Parliament; restored bursaries; safe staffing; reversed marketisation; new health spending watchdog; free hospital parking funded by a PMI tax rise. Social care: £8bn more over the Parliament (including £1bn in year one), Ethical Care Charter implementation, higher Carer’s Allowance, and foundations for a National Care Service with a cap on lifetime costs and free end‑of‑life care.

Education: a National Education Service with free lifelong FE, restored EMA, free ESOL, higher FE funding, quality‑assured apprenticeships, and a commission on lifelong learning. Schools to receive restored funding, smaller early‑years class sizes, universal primary free meals (funded by VAT on private school fees), SEND strategy, and expanded counselling. Higher education tuition fees abolished and maintenance grants restored. Early years: expanded free childcare (including all two‑year‑olds), workforce professionalisation, and revived Sure Start.

Security and justice: 10,000 additional community police officers; review of Prevent; 500 more border guards; 3,000 more firefighters and prison officers; legal aid restorations; no‑fault divorce; environmental tribunal; rehabilitation‑focused prisons; review of probation part‑privatisation.

Transport: public ownership of rail as franchises expire; fare caps, free on‑train Wi‑Fi, accessibility duties; local powers to regulate buses and create municipal operators; support for low‑emission vehicles, cleaner buses, cycling and walking; road safety targets; Severn tolls removal; airport capacity subject to air, noise and climate tests.

Environment and animal welfare: a new Clean Air Act, habitat and “blue belt” protections, deposit‑return schemes, neonicotinoid ban, 1m native trees, stronger anti‑cruelty penalties, bans on third‑party puppy sales and ivory trade, and retention of hunting bans.

Culture, media, and sport: a £1bn Cultural Capital Fund, free national museums, an arts pupil premium, media plurality and Leveson reforms, supporter representation in football governance, accessible stadia, grassroots reinvestment, and action on ticket‑touting.

Devolution, equality, and constitution: a Constitutional Convention; votes at 16; stronger FOI; tighter lobbying rules; reform of the second chamber; enhanced EHRC powers; gender and ethnicity pay action; updated trans protections; LGBT‑inclusive RSE; recognition of BSL; terminal illness as a protected characteristic.

Foreign, defence, and development: multilateral diplomacy, recognition of Palestine alongside Israel’s security, suspension of arms exports where IHL risks exist (with a Yemen inquiry), a strategic defence review, NATO 2% spending floor, renewal of nuclear deterrent with disarmament aims, a defence industrial strategy, improved forces’ conditions, 0.7% ODA maintained, SDG delivery, action on tax havens with public registers, support for universal health coverage, and R&D on global diseases.
